_comment: Bean d5f1. One agent's INSPECTION of every extracted image, as data rather than code, so the judgement can be reviewed line by line and re-run. `saw` is the REASON for the role, not the description; `draft` is the description. Every entry here was produced by looking at the image. Applied by scripts/apply-image-verdicts.ts, which writes an `inspection` basis naming this agent and leaves every narrative in `draft` — only a human may confirm one (schemas/narrative.ts). SPLIT 2026-09-20 (bean frs5): this file judged documents that now live in TWO libraries, so it became two files, each beside the documents it judges. A single verdict file spanning libraries is how one library's judgement comes to rewrite another's `images.json` -- `apply-image-verdicts` resolves each document against the library its verdict file is IN, and could not do that from one shared file. Nothing was re-judged: every verdict below is byte-identical to the one it was split from, and `inspected_by`/`inspected_at` are carried over unchanged because the inspection they record actually happened, once, before the split.

img-p126-1.draft: The GRADE approach to rating confidence in an estimate of effect. Rows give study design — randomized controlled trials, which start at high confidence, and observational studies, which start at low. Between them, five reasons for lowering confidence (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias) and three for raising it (large effect, dose response, and plausible confounding that would either reduce a demonstrated effect or suggest a spurious one). The right-hand column gives the four resulting levels — high, moderate, low and very low — each shown with the circle notation, from four filled circles down to one.

img-p154-1.saw: a comparison table of four rapid-review types
img-p154-1.draft: A comparison of four types of rapid review — a traditional systematic review conducted rapidly, a rapid review of systematic reviews, a rapid review of systematic reviews plus primary studies, and a rapid review of primary studies only — across twelve methodological dimensions. The traditional review allows up to 16 weeks where the three rapid forms allow up to 12. It differs from them throughout: no restrictions on literature search or number of databases against restrictions and 2–3 databases; complete data-extraction verification against one reviewer with selected verification; outcomes restricted to four or fewer against two to four with more if available. Rows also cover question types, number of questions, use of systematic reviews, grey literature, screening, study designs included, risk-of-bias assessment, and assessment of the quality of the body of evidence.

vfig-p015.saw: Fig 5, the seven-phase DIIG planning chart with resource tiles, 'WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture' highlighted
vfig-p015.draft: Fig 5, 'DIIG process for planning and implementing a digital health enterprise'. Seven numbered, colour-coded phases — from 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment to 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. To the right, resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked as PDF or online, including the WHO–ITU eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide, the ITU SDG digital investment framework, TOGAF, OpenHIE, the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits, and the WHO MAPS toolkit. 'WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture (this document)' is highlighted twice: spanning phases 02 to 04, and in phase 07. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

vfig-p032.saw: a boxed TEXT panel — Step 2 'Define a target DHSC architecture' with inputs, tasks, outputs, resources, a best-practice note and a risks table — whose text is in the extracted sections; the page's 'Fig. 14' is a cross-reference and no figure is drawn. Filed as decorative for want of a text-panel role
vfig-p032.draft: Step 2 panel, 'Define a target DHSC architecture': inputs, tasks, outputs and resources boxes, a best-practice note on capturing consumption at the last mile, and a table of potential risks and mitigation strategies.

vfig-p034.saw: Fig 14, the DHSC architecture: services, interoperability layer and supply-chain systems with explanatory callouts
vfig-p034.draft: Fig 14, 'DHSC architecture framework'. Inside a frame labelled DIGITAL HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN ENTERPRISE: SHARED SERVICES (foundational components: facility, product and supplier registries), DATA SERVICES (analytics — supply chain reports, data warehouse; traceability — track and trace, product verification) and Digital ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). Below them, an INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. At the bottom, HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS (forecasting and planning, order, warehouse and cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing), beside EXTERNAL SYSTEMS (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Callouts explain each layer — for example, that OpenHIM is a useful reference for interoperability components, and SCISMM and TSS v2 for the supply chain systems.

vfig-p040.saw: Fig 19, the DHSC architecture with supply-chain information systems split across national, district and facility levels; the page's 'Fig. 20' candidate is a cross-reference
vfig-p040.draft: Fig 19, 'Architecture based on supply chain design: decentralized management (option B)'. The DHSC architecture — shared services, data services, digital ecosystems, an interoperability layer of enabling components, and external systems — with its health supply chain information systems divided by level. At national level: forecasting and planning, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management, warehouse management and cold chain management. At district level: procurement, order management, inventory management and cold chain management. At facility level: dispensing.

vfig-p041.saw: Fig 20, transactional data from a supply-chain flow rising through the interoperability layer into analytics services, with the questions they answer
vfig-p041.draft: Fig 20, 'Benefits of cross-enterprise analytics services'. Along the bottom runs the physical supply chain: manufacturing, shipping, regulatory customs, central-warehouse receiving and inventory management, distribution, regional-warehouse replenishment, health-facility dispensing, and patients. Above it sit the planning processes: forecasting and planning; supplier and contract management; procurement; and order management. Dashed arrows carry 'Transactional data from systems relevant to the supply chain' up through the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER into DATA SERVICES — analytics: supply chain reports and a data warehouse. A callout lists the questions analytics services answer: optimizing inventory against consumption to minimize stockouts, whether planned supplies will arrive in time, forecast accuracy against actual consumption, on-time and in-full delivery, wastage and leakage, stock at risk of expiry and where to move it, where and how often stockouts occur, and supplier performance.

vfig-p049.saw: Fig 23, total cost of ownership grouped into implement, scale, operate and ongoing cost components; the crop also takes in the Step 3 text panel above it
vfig-p049.draft: Fig 23, 'Cost components to determine the total cost of ownership'. A dashed loop labelled 'Total cost of ownership' encloses four groups of cost components. IMPLEMENT: sourcing (RFP, RFI, RFQ), software, hardware and infrastructure, design and development, integration and interoperability, testing and training, and deployment. SCALE: expansion of deployment, training, and hardware and infrastructure. OPERATE: software subscriptions, maintenance (personnel, software, hardware), ongoing training, and monitoring and evaluation. ONGOING: management, governance and overhead. Adapted from the 2020 WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide.

vfig-p055.saw: Fig 24, supply-chain systems at each location exchanging data through the interoperability layer with traceability services; the page's 'Fig. 25' is a cross-reference
vfig-p055.draft: Fig 24, 'Achieving track and trace capabilities through DHSC architecture components'. Along the bottom, the supply chain runs from regulator through central, regional and district warehouses to health facilities and patients. Each location's system — regulator systems, warehouse management, transportation management, inventory management, dispensing, and verification at the patient — exchanges data in both directions with the INTEROPERABILITY LAYER, as do the external systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories). Above the layer, DATA SERVICES hold analytics and traceability (track and trace, product verification). A callout lists the questions traceability services answer: where a batch is now, whether supply chain integrity was maintained, who had custody on a date, where a batch was dispensed, whether the product moved through known locations, whether there were anomalies, and whether the product is genuine. A legend defines traceability data as what (product, batch and serial number), when, where and why (the transaction type).

vfig-p056.saw: Fig 25, a mock track-and-trace screen for one batch above the event flow that feeds it
vfig-p056.draft: Fig 25, 'Illustrative example of a traceability service interface'. At the top is a mock screen, 'Track and trace results for product 001001123123', batch A1001234. It shows a timeline of five verified events with their location and timestamp: verified and received at the central warehouse (11 Mar 2023); shipped from the central warehouse (5 Apr); verified and received at health facility 001 (6 Apr); verified and dispensed there (10 Apr); and a final patient-side verification of serial number 202 with GPS coordinates (10 Apr, 16:14). Below, the flow that produces it: the manufacturer, central/regional warehouse and health facilities emit ship, receive and dispense events, and handheld verify scans are made along the way. All of these feed DATA SERVICES (analytics and traceability), which answer the screen's query for the product code, batch, its serial numbers 201 to 204 and the expiry date.

vfig-p011.saw: Fig 1, three nested circles of supply chain processes with partner icons on their rims
vfig-p011.draft: Fig 1, 'Public health supply chain partners and processes'. Four nested circles. The outer blue circle holds forecasting and planning and traceability, with the Ministry of health, regulators, procurers, manufacturers/distributors and logistics providers on or near its rim. The orange circle holds sourcing and contract management, procurement and transportation/shipping. The purple circle holds warehouse management, order management and transportation/distribution, with central and regional warehouses on its rim. The innermost green circle holds dispensing, with community health, health facilities and individuals at the centre.

Eight rounded boxes: forecasting and planning, sourcing and contract management, order management, traceability, procurement, warehouse management, transportation and dispensing. Two-headed arrows join them, showing that information flows both ways between the processes; warehouse management is the most connected box.

vfig-p013.saw: Fig 3, six hexagons around 'Individuals' inside a dashed ring of partners
vfig-p013.draft: Fig 3, 'Digital health supply chain'. Six purple hexagons surround an icon labelled Individuals: digital ecosystem, end-to-end visibility, data and analytics, transactional systems, advanced digitization and collaborative processes. A dashed ring around them carries eleven partners as dots: Ministry of health, community health, health facilities, regional warehouses, private sector, central warehouse, regulators, logistics providers, procurers and manufacturers/distributors.

vfig-p014.saw: Fig 4, four chevrons for the handbook's chapters with their numbered steps; the crop also takes in body text above it
vfig-p014.draft: Fig 4, 'The stepwise approach used in this handbook'. Four coloured chevrons in a row: 1. Defining a holistic DHSC strategy; 2. Defining the DHSC architecture; 3. Planning for scalable implementation and sustainable operations; 4. Using the DHSC to implement traceability. Chevron 1 lists four steps (identify and engage stakeholders, analyse the current state of HSCISs, define the vision and strategic goals, define a strategic roadmap and performance indicators). Chevron 2 lists three (assess the current state of HSCISs, define a target architecture, identify implementation activities and map them to strategic goals). Chevron 3 lists four (plan the implementation, develop an operational plan, develop a budget, and implement each intervention). The crop also includes the chapter list and a 'Before using this handbook' box above the figure.

vfig-p016.saw: Fig 6, SMART Guidelines L1-L5 knowledge layers above their country adaptations, with feedback arrows
vfig-p016.draft: Fig 6, 'WHO SMART Guidelines approach'. A top band of five knowledge layers, each fed from a research and evidence base: L1 narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 machine-readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 executable (reference software) and L5 dynamic (precision health models). A localisation bar leads down to five matching country adaptations: national policies and procedures, localized requirements, localized machine-readable code and standards, localized digital services, and dynamic applications trained for local outcomes. These feed data, evidence and impact, and an 'Evidence from digital implementations' arrow returns to the research base. Source: adapted from WHO SMART Guidelines.

vfig-p017.saw: Fig 7, the ANC DAK BPMN swimlane workflow with supply-chain-related tasks outlined, plus an enlarged inset
vfig-p017.draft: Fig 7, 'Sample workflow for an antenatal care business, with connections to the supply chain highlighted'. A BPMN diagram with client and health worker lanes: arrival, registration, rapid assessment, danger signs, pregnancy confirmation, quick check, profile and history, the ANC assessment group, the counselling and treatment group (10.1 to 10.9), referral, scheduling and self-care. An enlarged inset shows the tasks outlined in purple as connected to the supply chain: 9 conduct laboratory tests and imaging, 10.5 nutrition supplementation, 10.7 immunizations and 10.9 deworming and malaria counselling and prophylaxis. Source: adapted from the 2021 WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for Antenatal Care.

vfig-p020.draft: Fig 8, 'Alignment of national strategies'. Nested arrow shapes, each ending in VISION. The health strategy contains the health supply chain strategy, which contains the medicines and health product strategy. The digital/IT strategy contains the digital health strategy. The digital health supply chain strategy sits where the two families overlap.

vfig-p021.draft: Fig 9, 'Inconsistent use of standardized product nomenclature across the supply chain'. img-p030-1.saw: a stepped diagram of product packaging levels
img-p030-1.draft: Fig. 10, 'Product packaging hierarchy' (source: GS1.org), in the section on instituting data management and governance policies. It is drawn as a staircase of four grey steps, each holding packaging illustrations. The top step, labelled PRIMARY, shows individual items such as vials, a bottle, syringes in blister packs, a blister strip and a sterile-packed instrument. The next step, SECONDARY, shows boxes and cartons holding those items; the third, SECONDARY OR TERTIARY, shows open cartons and a row of boxed packs; and the bottom step, TERTIARY, shows shipping cases and a shrink-wrapped pallet of boxes.

vfig-p010.saw: Fig. 1, a health product linked to four circles of product master data; the crop also takes in the section heading and two paragraphs of body prose above it, because the figure's background panel bleeds off the page
vfig-p010.draft: Fig. 1, 'Product master data'. A health product, drawn as a boxed medicine package, is linked to PRODUCT MASTER DATA, shown as four categories with examples. General Information: product identifier, name, description, unit of measure. Classification: ICD, ATC, product characteristics/specifications. Pharmaceutical Information: dosage, strength, route of administration, doses per vial. Logistical Information: packaging, volumetrics, shelf life, storage temperature.

vfig-p011.saw: Fig. 2, partners and processes both feeding a central product-master-data column, flowing down to patients
vfig-p011.draft: Fig. 2, 'Importance of product master data'. Three columns. On the left, SUPPLY CHAIN PARTNERS: manufacturers, procurers, Ministry of Health / programmes, donors, shippers, regulatory authority, central/regional/district warehouses and health facilities. On the right, SUPPLY CHAIN PROCESSES: forecasting and supply planning, procurement, ordering/re-ordering, inventory management, distribution, dispensing, product recalls and finance/insurance. Arrows from both point into the central PRODUCT MASTER DATA column — general information, classification details, pharmaceutical information, logistical information and other information — which flows down through a medicine icon to Patients.

vfig-p012.saw: Fig. 3, the physical flow of products across actors, each system holding a different product code joined by broken links
vfig-p012.draft: Fig. 3, 'Impact of inconsistent product information'. An arrow labelled PHYSICAL FLOW OF HEALTH PRODUCTS runs across five actors: manufacturers, central warehouse, health facilities, community health workers and patients. Beneath them sit the systems each stage uses — a warehouse management system, an eLMIS and paper forms — and each holds the same product under a different code (123123, A1232, P44545, AM545). Broken-chain icons join the codes, showing that the identifiers do not link up along the chain.

vfig-p013.saw: Fig. 4, the seven-phase digital-health planning chart with resource tiles, this document highlighted in phase 07
vfig-p013.draft: Fig. 4, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases — assessing the current state and enabling environment; establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; defining the future state; planning the enterprise architecture; determining health content requirements; M&E and fostering data use; and implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. Resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked as PDF or online, among them the DIIG, the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits, TOGAF, OpenHIE and the WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture. The tile 'WHO handbook for health product catalogue (this document)' is highlighted in phase 07. It is the same chart as Fig. 6 of the WHO handbook for digitalizing primary health care, re-pointed to this document.

vfig-p014.saw: Fig. 5, the SMART Guidelines five-layer diagram with localisation and an evidence feedback loop
vfig-p014.draft: Fig. 5, 'WHO SMART Guidelines Approach'. A research and evidence base feeds five knowledge layers and their products: L1 Narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 Machine readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 Executable (reference software) and L5 Dynamic (precision health models). Each passes through LOCALISATION into a country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures, localised requirements, localised machine-readable code and standards, localised static digital services, and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. All feed DATA, EVIDENCE, AND IMPACT, which returns to the evidence base as EVIDENCE FROM DIGITAL IMPLEMENTATIONS.

vfig-p015.saw: Fig. 6, an ANC BPMN swimlane workflow with an enlarged inset of its assessment and counselling activities, some highlighted
vfig-p015.draft: Fig. 6, 'Example of an Antenatal Care Business clinical workflow with highlighted' activities. The upper part is a swimlane process in a health facility, with Client and Health worker lanes. The client arrives at the facility, then goes through registration, rapid assessment and management, a danger-signs/referral decision, pregnancy confirmation, a first-contact decision and a quick check. These lead to collecting the woman's profile and history, then an ANC assessment (check symptoms and follow-up, conduct physical exam, conduct laboratory tests and imaging), then 10. Counselling, in-facility management and treatment, with subactivities 10.1 to 10.9, then a referral decision, scheduling, and self-care in the home or community until the woman returns. The lower part enlarges activities 6 to 10. Highlighted borders mark 9 (conduct laboratory tests and imaging), 10.5 nutrition supplementation, 10.7 immunizations and 10.9 deworming and malaria counselling and prophylaxis — the activities that involve health products.

vfig-p016.saw: Fig. 7, a layered architecture with shared/data services, an interoperability layer and supply-chain information systems
vfig-p016.draft: Fig. 7, 'Digital health supply chain architecture framework'. Top row: SHARED SERVICES, whose foundational components are facility, product (highlighted) and supplier registries; DATA SERVICES, with analytics (supply chain reports, data warehouse) and traceability (track and trace, product verification); and Digital Ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). A middle INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. Bottom: HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS — forecasting and planning, order management, warehouse management, cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing — beside External systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories).

vfig-p028.saw: Fig. 8, three columns from classification to product to trade items, with a paracetamol example; the crop clips the rotated row labels at its left edge
vfig-p028.draft: Fig. 8, 'Linkage across classifications, generic products and trade items'. Three columns: CLASSIFICATION (classes or groups of diseases, pathogens or drugs); PRODUCT (name/INN, strength, dosage form, route of administration); and TRADE ITEM (unique identifier such as a GTIN, brand name, manufacturer, country of origin, packaging details, volumetrics, shelf life). The example row traces Nervous system → Analgesics → Other analgesics and antipyretics → Anilides → Paracetamol to the product 'Paracetamol 500 mg tablet'. That product branches into two manufacturers' trade items, each with its own unique IDs and pack hierarchy: a case and inner pack of 100 from ABC Manufacturing (brand Ceta123), and a case, inner pack of 50 and each of 10 from XYZ Manufacturing (brand ParaXYZ). A bottom row gives each column's use: strategic (data aggregation and analysis), tactical (forecasting, procurement planning and aggregate visibility) and operational (inventory, distribution, tracking and tracing, pharmacovigilance and AEFI analysis).

vfig-p029.saw: Fig. 9, a three-class data model with attribute cardinalities and 1-to-0..* associations
vfig-p029.draft: Fig. 9, 'Relationship between generic product, trade item and regulated trade item'. Three classes are drawn as boxes listing their attributes with cardinalities. GENERIC PRODUCT has identifier 0..*, status, name (nameType, nameValue), description, classification, unitOfUse, dosageForm, strength, routeOfAdministration, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, doseQuantity, attribute (type, value[x]) and associatedProduct (product, relationship, quantity). TRADE ITEM has identifier 1..*, status, tradeItemName, description, classification, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, associatedGenericProduct (genericProduct, quantity), contains (tradeItem, quantity) and attribute. REGULATED TRADE ITEM has identifier, status, jurisdiction, authorisationHolder, validityPeriod, authorisedTradeItem, attribute and associatedProduct. The associations read: one generic product to zero or more trade items, and one trade item to zero or more regulated trade items.

vfig-p030.saw: TWO figures, Fig. 10 and Fig. 11, in one crop beneath a WHODrug text panel that the crop also takes in
vfig-p030.draft: Fig. 10, 'Product packaging hierarchy', shows four stepped shelves of packaged goods labelled, top to bottom, PRIMARY (vials, syringes, blister packs), SECONDARY, SECONDARY OR TERTIARY, and TERTIARY (cases and pallets). Source: GS1.org. Fig. 11, 'Example of packaging variations across manufacturers', shows one PRODUCT, a paracetamol 500 mg tablet, procured from two manufacturers with different pack configurations: MFR A ships 1 case of 12 packs of 50 tablets each, and MFR B ships 1 case of 10 packs of 100 tablets each.

vfig-p031.saw: Fig. 12, a generic product linked to manufacturers' trade items through a pallet→case→inner-pack chain; the crop also takes in the next section's 'Step 3' heading band
vfig-p031.draft: Fig. 12, 'Mapping across product packaging hierarchy using FHIR resource'. Five record boxes, each listing identifier, description, name, characteristic and association. A GENERIC PRODUCT (identifier MR001) associates to a trade item from manufacturer A (identifier 17801415202675) and to manufacturer B's tertiary pallet (18901415202906). The pallet associates to MFR B's tertiary case (08901415202908, quantity 100), which associates to MFR B's secondary inner pack (08901415202910, quantity 50) — the packaging hierarchy expressed as chained associations.

vfig-p040.saw: Fig. 13, a national product code record branching to two GTIN/trade-item tables; whole page checked at low resolution and the crop holds the whole figure
vfig-p040.draft: Fig. 13, 'Transitional approach to adopting globally unique trade item numbers'. A national product code record — NPC01101001, Lamivudine 50 mg tablet, dosage form TA, route oral — branches into two tables of trade items mapped to it. The first holds GS1 GTINs (for example 58904093825793) for manufacturer MFR001 from IN, with child GTINs, child quantities of 100 and 10, 3000 eaches and a shelf life of 670. The second holds items from MFR002 from KE that have no GTIN yet and are identified only by country trade item identifiers (P006008, P006009), with child quantities of 120 and 30, 7200 eaches and a shelf life of 1095. So a national code can carry GTIN-identified and not-yet-GTIN-identified items side by side during the transition.

vfig-p017.draft: Fig. 1.1.1, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. vfig-p019.draft: Fig. 1.1.4, 'Essential processes of national digital health implementations'. A left-to-right flow runs DIGITAL HEALTH STRATEGY → INVESTMENT ROADMAP → ENTERPRISE ARCHITECTURE → APPLICATION WITH INTERVENTIONS → SCALE, INSTITUTIONALIZE AND SUSTAIN, with a feedback arrow from scaling back to applications. Inputs feed in from above: national health priorities (into the strategy), the national inventory of digital assets (exchanged with the roadmap and architecture) and health-programme-specific needs. Governance mechanisms and a data use culture support from below, and the digital maturity of the country informs the strategy. A shaded region labelled DIIG encloses the architecture, applications and scaling steps — the part this guide covers. At the bottom sit the national eHealth strategy building blocks: leadership and governance; strategy and investment; legislation, policy and compliance; workforce; infrastructure; standards and interoperability; and services and applications.

vfig-p043.saw: Fig. 3.1, three columns — Think, Rethink, Describe — for analysis, redesign and requirements; the caption itself sits outside the crop
vfig-p043.draft: Fig. 3.1, 'Adaptation of CRDM approach for defining health system challenges' and requirements. Three columns. BUSINESS PROCESS ANALYSIS, 'Think — how do we do our work now?': define goals and objectives, determine the health programme processes to target, map the user journey and workflow, and identify pain points. BUSINESS PROCESS REDESIGN, 'Rethink — how should we do our work now?': examine tasks and workflow, identify inefficiencies, restructure them, and select digital health interventions for the prioritized health system challenges. REQUIREMENTS DEFINITION, 'Describe — how can an information system support our work?': define the tasks for the optimized processes, describe how business rules are implemented, check that the enabling environment can support the interventions, define what the interventions should do from end-user needs, and determine whether existing ICT systems can be leveraged.

vfig-p044.saw: Fig. 3.1.1.1, a process matrix table; the crop also takes in the section heading and body prose. NOTE: the caption says 'three example processes' but the table holds FOUR (A–D) — a discrepancy in the source, recorded rather than corrected
vfig-p044.draft: Fig. 3.1.1.1, 'Process matrix illustrating three example processes within a typical vaccination programme'. A table with the columns Process, Objective, Task set and Outcomes, holding four rows. A Patient management keeps a database of all newborns and their vaccination history (register, search, maintain), leading to more complete registration. B Vaccination management ensures every infant receives all scheduled doses (define the schedule, plan, send reminders, register vaccinations, monitor coverage), leading to more timely vaccination and higher coverage. C Stock management keeps vaccines available while minimizing wastage (order, receive, store, count, monitor balances and expiry), leading to higher availability and lower wastage. D Service delivery ensures quality vaccination services (counsel, diagnose, dispense, refer, update the record, schedule the next visit), leading to correct protocol, timelier vaccinations and better documentation.

vfig-p057.draft: Fig. 4.1, 'Redesigning health programme processes'. Here the redesign and requirements columns are boxed together under the label 'Chapter 4', marking the part of the approach the chapter covers.

vfig-p064.saw: Fig. 4.2.1, the eHealth building blocks grouped into enabling and ICT environments, each with its contributions
vfig-p064.draft: Fig. 4.2.1, 'Roles and contributions of component “building blocks”' to a national eHealth environment. Two groups of building blocks, each block paired with its contributions. ENABLING ENVIRONMENT: leadership, governance and multisector engagement (direct and coordinate eHealth nationally, align with health goals, support change); strategy and investment (a responsive national strategy and plan, with financing aligned to priorities); legislation, policy and compliance (national policies and a legal and enforcement environment that builds trust); workforce (eHealth knowledge and skills, networks, and education and training programmes); and standards and interoperability (consistent, accurate collection and exchange of health information). ICT ENVIRONMENT: infrastructure (networks, core services and applications for information exchange across boundaries) and services and applications (the means of delivering health content and managing information, for the public, patients, providers and others).

vfig-p073.saw: Fig. 4.5.1, a five-row checklist of design considerations, each with its guiding questions; the caption sits outside the crop
vfig-p073.draft: Fig. 4.5.1, 'Considerations for designing a digital health enterprise'. A checklist of five ticked considerations, each with guiding questions. Identified pain points and health system challenges: what challenges did the stakeholders identify, and are digital interventions appropriate or should non-digital approaches also be considered? Evidence base and experience with the digital health intervention(s): has it been shown to address the challenges, will more than one be needed, and has it been tested at the necessary scale? Enabling environment: can the enabling and ICT environment support it, and what precautions are needed (see Chapter 5)? Requirements: how well does the enterprise meet user needs and stakeholder expectations, and does it fit the existing culture, language and workflows? Linkages to other ICT enterprises: are other interventions being implemented in the context, and can they be leveraged?

vfig-p078.draft: Fig. 5.1, 'Essential components of a digital health implementation'. Dotted lines tie this to the SERVICES & APPLICATIONS block of a foundational layer, 'ICT and Enabling Environment', made of the building blocks: leadership and governance across the top, above strategy and investment; services and applications; standards and interoperability; infrastructure; legislation, policy and compliance; and workforce.

vfig-p101.saw: Fig. 6.3.2, the OpenHIE layered architecture with a numbered ten-item legend; the crop also takes in Box 6.3.1 above it
vfig-p101.draft: Fig. 6.3.2, 'OpenHIE architectural diagram illustrating mechanisms for interoperability across different applications'. Within a DIGITAL HEALTH PLATFORM, the OpenHIE component layer holds business domain services — (1) logistics management information system, (2) shared health record and (3) health management information system — and registry services — (4) terminology services, (5) client registry, (6) facility registry, (7) health worker registry and (8) product registry. Beneath them, (9) the interoperability services layer provides authentication, an interlinking service and entity mapping. Below the platform sit (10) point-of-service applications: mobile system, electronic medical record, health management information system, lab, pharmacy and logistics management information system. A legend defines each numbered component — for example, that the interoperability layer receives all communications from external services and orchestrates data exchange with the component layer. vfig-p015.saw: Fig. 1, a staircase diagram above a four-column comparison table
vfig-p015.draft: Fig. 1, 'From paper to digital: a transformational journey'. The upper half is a rising staircase of four stages, each an icon and a heading — PAPER, DIGITIZATION, DIGITALIZATION, DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION — joined by arrows labelled 'From paper to digital', 'Improve existing processes' and 'Fundamentally change healthcare delivery'. A vertical axis, 'Data use', runs from 'Limited data use with little to no interoperability standards adopted' at the bottom to 'Greater data use with greater adoption of interoperability standards' at the top; a horizontal arrow beneath is labelled 'Process Optimization'. The lower half is a table with one column per stage (Paper, Digitization, Digitalization, Digital transformation) and five rows: Definition, Examples, Benefits, Challenges and Dependencies. For example, Paper is defined as manually capturing and processing data in paper formats, with examples such as paper register books and tally sheets; Digital transformation is defined as digitally optimizing and driving systems-level change through innovation, analytics and feedback mechanisms, with examples such as algorithms for personalized treatment plans.

vfig-p017.saw: Fig. 3, four nested rounded layers around the care seeker with digital-solution icons in each
vfig-p017.draft: Fig. 3, 'Delivering an integrated ecosystem of information systems and digital health solutions supports the PHC approach'. Four nested layers surround a figure labelled 'Centered around the needs of the care seeker'. From innermost to outermost: COMMUNITY LINKAGES AND ENGAGEMENT (community health workers, care seekers) holds patient portal, targeted messaging, CHW job aid, self-monitoring devices and capacity building; ORGANIZATION AND MANAGEMENT (primary care providers) holds clinical job aids, AI risk assessment, referral and coordination, and an electronic health record; SELECTION, DESIGN AND PLANNING OF SERVICES (health system decision makers) holds a dashboard and management information systems; DEFINING A TARGET POPULATION AND UNDERSTANDING THEIR NEEDS (policy makers) holds civil registration and vital statistics, and disease surveillance. Each solution carries a one-line purpose. A note says solutions can span more than one layer and are allocated to one only for illustration.

vfig-p019.saw: Fig. 4, a five-tier stack of data uses with a person at the base
vfig-p019.draft: Fig. 4, 'The added value of “collect once, use for many purposes” principle'. Five stacked tiers rise from a person icon at the base. Bottom to top: Primary, individual data collection (clinical, lab, pharmacy, registries and ID data); Person-centred health service delivery (clinical decision support, scheduling, case management); Programme management (operational decision support, quality improvement, facility management, process optimization); Health system monitoring (national strategic plans and policies, national indicators, accountability); and Global monitoring (accountability towards the SDGs). A side bar groups the lower two tiers as 'Primary data use' and the upper three as 'Secondary data use'.

vfig-p020.saw: Fig. 5, five knowledge layers L1–L5 flowing through localisation to country adaptation
vfig-p020.draft: Fig. 5, 'WHO SMART Guidelines approach'. Each layer passes through a 'Localisation' bar into a matching country-implementation adaptation: national policies and guidelines (L1), localised requirements (L2), localised machine-readable code and standards (L3), localised static digital services (L4) and dynamic digital applications optimised for local outcomes (L5). All five feed 'Data, evidence, and impact', which loops back to the evidence base as 'Evidence from digital implementations'.

vfig-p024.saw: Fig. 6, seven colour-coded phases with steps and a grid of linked resources
vfig-p024.draft: Fig. 6, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases run down the left: 01 Assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 Establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 Defining the future state; 04 Planning the enterprise architecture; 05 Determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 Implementing, maintaining and scaling. Each phase lists its steps, for example 'Develop a national digital health strategy' in phase 02 and 'Identify validated health content appropriate for the implementation context' in phase 05. vfig-p026.saw: Fig. 7, three successive iteration loops along a release arrow
vfig-p026.draft: Fig. 7, 'Iterative and agile approach'. Three circular loops sit along a horizontal timeline arrow: Minimum viable product (MVP), then VERSION 1, then VERSION 2. Each loop has the same four stages: understand and prioritize user requirements, design (adapt design in later versions), build and test, and train users. Milestones along the arrow read: determine that a PCPOSS is an appropriate health intervention; repeat the previous loop until meeting MVP specs to deploy; deploy and roll out; gather and manage user feedback; deploy and roll out; gather and manage user feedback; deploy, roll out and scale; and iterations for continuous improvement.

vfig-p032.saw: Fig. 8, an inverted pyramid of interview stages from broad to narrow with example prompts
vfig-p032.draft: Fig. 8, 'Example prompts and questions for starting broad and narrowing down'. An inverted pyramid of four bands runs from BROAD (start here) at the top to NARROW (end here) at the tip: TRUST BUMP, BIRD'S EYE VIEW, MAGNIFYING GLASS and MICRO-SCOPE. Beside each band are example interview prompts for health workers: intent and introductions ('Tell me about your background… as a health worker'); 'Tell me about the last time you… registered a new client / provided antenatal care / provided a routine immunization to a child'; 'Can you tell me more… about how you check for malaria?' and 'Can you show me how you… would fill out a paper register now?'; and the 5 Whys ('Why do you… wait until the end of the day to fill out your records?'), continued until a root cause is revealed. It closes with 'Express gratitude for health worker's time'. Adapted from Tran, 2018, under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

vfig-p035.saw: Fig. 9, a five-column table of family-planning business processes A–C
vfig-p035.draft: Fig. 9, 'Example business process matrix from family planning DAK'. A table with the columns Process name, Process ID, Personas, Objectives and Task set, the header row defining each column. Three processes follow. A Registration (FP.A), with client and clerk or health-care provider, ensures the client is in the system and queued for counselling; its tasks are to search for, review and update, or create a client record. B Family planning counselling (FP.B), with client and health-care provider, discusses methods and selects one the client is medically eligible for; its tasks run from taking a history and a risk assessment through checking medical eligibility criteria and stock to referral if the facility cannot provide the method. C Service provision (FP.C) provides the chosen method, covering informed consent, start timing, dual protection and follow-up scheduling. Source: WHO (30).

vfig-p038.saw: TWO figures on one page — the Fig. 10 swimlane workflow and the Fig. 11 annotation panel — and the crop also takes in the body prose and a TIP box between and below them, because their drawn frames span the page
vfig-p038.draft: Fig. 10, 'Workflow A: Registration business process', is a BPMN-style swimlane diagram. The pool is 'Health facility', with lanes Client and Health worker or Clerk. The client arrives at the facility (1), then rapid assessment and management (2) leads to 'Urgent referral necessary?' (3); Yes ends in C. ANC referral. No leads to gather client details (4), then search for client (5) and 'Match found?' (6). No leads to create client record (7); Yes leads to a grouped subprocess 8, Validate client details: review sociodemographic data with the client (8.1), 'Update needed?' (8.2), then update client details (8.3). Both paths reach check-in client (9), ending in B. ANC contact. Fig. 11, 'Notes and annotations for Workflow A: Registration business process', is a three-column text panel that annotates each numbered activity of Fig. 10 — for example, that rapid assessment is outside the DAK's scope, and the identifiers a client may present when searched for. Both cite WHO (29).

vfig-p042.saw: Fig. 12, a three-question flow with explanation and action columns
vfig-p042.draft: Fig. 12, 'Is each and every data element collected truly needed?'. Three rows, each reading Question → Explanation → Action to be taken, with arrows chaining each row's action into the next question. 1. Is the data element duplicated? Duplicates may share a definition under different labels, or be collected on several forms; reconcile them into one element collected once. 2. Is the data element needed for service delivery or accountability? Ask whether it supports clinical decision-making, mandatory reporting or accountability; if not, consider removing it to reduce the data-entry burden on health workers. 3. Is the data element orphaned? Orphaned data is hard to use without its context; link it to its primary data elements (anything not needed will already have gone at question 2).

vfig-p045.draft: Fig. 13, 'Example decision-support logic matrix from DAK for HIV'. A table with four columns: activity ID and name, decision table ID, decision table description, and reference/source. It has six rows, HIV.DT.01 to HIV.DT.06: check for serious illness; test for HIV using the testing algorithm; determine retest recommendation; PrEP eligibility check; determine PEP or PrEP regimen; and screen for TB. Each row cites the WHO consolidated guideline section it is drawn from — for example the 2019 consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, and its figures on universal HIV testing and early infant diagnosis. Source: WHO (31).

vfig-p046.saw: Fig. 14, a branching decision tree from antenatal registration on HIV status and risk
vfig-p046.draft: Fig. 14, 'Decision-support logic for a clinical care pathway in the form of a decision tree'. It starts at 'Antenatal registration — provider-initiated HIV testing & counselling' and splits on the result. HIV-positive leads to PMTCT, treatment, support and an offer of partner notification, then partner testing. Partner HIV-negative leads to reassessing the woman's risk and offering partner referral for VMMC. Partner not tested or HIV-positive leads to offering the partner HIV treatment (if positive), condom promotion and risk-reduction counselling. HIV-negative leads to standard post-test guidance and counselling on prevention, then two branches: offer partner testing and a risk assessment (which feeds partner testing), and a risk assessment using a tool. That tool separates a woman at substantial risk of HIV acquisition from one who is not. At substantial risk, she is offered comprehensive prevention options — STI screening and treatment, condom promotion, risk-reduction counselling, PrEP with emphasis on adherence, and follow-up ANC visits. A woman who chooses to initiate PrEP then receives clinical laboratory assessments, adherence counselling, and emphasis on follow-up visits and repeat HIV testing. Source: WHO (29).

vfig-p054.saw: Fig. 15, three coloured phases on fidelity-versus-time axes with questions under each
vfig-p054.draft: Fig. 15, 'Levels of insight gained from different prototypes'. The vertical axis is level of prototype fidelity and the horizontal axis is the time required to develop the protocol. An arrow climbs through three phases: Validation, with low-fidelity prototypes (sketches, wireframes); Refinement, with moderate-fidelity prototypes (mockups); and Deployment, with higher-fidelity prototypes (clickable prototypes). Under each phase are the questions it answers. Validation asks: do users need this, and would this digital record solve their administrative reporting problems? Refinement asks: could it improve service delivery or accountability, and will users use it as intended? Deployment asks: does it have the key features, will users adopt it, and what behaviour change or roadblocks to adoption must be addressed? Adapted from Norman Tran/Stanford school (35).

img-p038-1.draft: An 'Instructions' panel of three steps for the health worker. img-p039-1.saw: the 'Which vaccines can be given today?' chart of vaccine columns against age rows
img-p039-1.draft: A chart titled 'Which vaccines can be given today?', with the line 'It is better to vaccinate late than never!'. Rows are ages (birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 9 months, 18 months, 2 years); coloured columns are vaccines, each starting at the age of its first dose and running downward as an arrow. HepB BD and BCG start at birth, HepB BD ending at a stop sign; OPV 1-3, PCV 1-3, Penta 1-3 and RV 1-3 at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, RV ending at a stop sign before 2 years; IPV at 14 weeks; MCV 1 at 9 months; DTP4 (or Penta4), MCV 2 and MenA at 18 months. A 'When to give' column gives the timing for each row (for example, at 10 weeks or as soon as possible thereafter, and at least 4 weeks after dose 1), and a 'When not to give' column gives the limits: HepB BD not after 6 weeks; RV1, RV2 and RV3 not after 2 years of age; later doses not before 4 weeks since the previous dose; MCV1 and MenA not before 9 months of age except where indicated. A footer says there is no need to restart a series after a long gap, and there is no upper age limit for most vaccines except rotavirus (under 2 years) and the hepatitis B birth dose (under 6 weeks).

vfig-p013.saw: Fig. 1, health content plus digital health interventions plus digital applications, above a foundational-layer grid
vfig-p013.draft: Fig. 1, 'Digital adaptation kits representing health content within broader needs for digital health implementations'. Three boxes are joined by plus signs: HEALTH CONTENT (information aligned with recommended health practices or validated health content), shown with the cover of this kit; DIGITAL HEALTH INTERVENTIONS (a discrete function of digital technology to achieve health-sector objectives); and DIGITAL APPLICATIONS (ICT systems and communication channels that facilitate delivery of the interventions and content). An orange frame encloses the three, and dotted lines run from it to the highlighted 'Services and applications' cell of a Foundational Layer (ICT and enabling environment) below, whose other cells are leadership and governance, strategy and investment, standards and interoperability, infrastructure, legislation, policy and compliance, and workforce. Source: adapted from reference 14.

vfig-p017.saw: Fig. 2, the five SMART layers L1-L5 on the left, each feeding a country L1-L5 adaptation on the right through a localisation bar
vfig-p017.draft: Fig. 2, 'Digital adaptation kits within the SMART guideline continuum'. Five rows: L1 Narrative (narrative guidelines: evidence-based recommendations with implementation and data guidance); L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits: software-neutral documentation of operational and functional requirements such as personas, workflows, metadata, algorithms, minimum data sets and priority metrics); L3 Machine readable (structured software-neutral specifications, code, terminology and interoperability standards); L4 Executable (reference software that executes static algorithms and interoperable components); and L5 Dynamic (precision health models trained and optimised with advanced analytics). Each row passes through a vertical 'Localisation' bar to its country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures; localised requirements; localised machine-readable code and standards; localised static digital services within a digital health enterprise; and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. A blue arrow beside them runs from 'Paper systems' at the top to 'Smart digital systems' at the bottom. Source: adapted from reference 18.

vfig-p024.saw: Fig. 3, seven coloured phases with their steps, beside a grid of resource tiles
vfig-p024.draft: Fig. 3, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases, each with its steps: 01 assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 defining the future state; 04 planning the enterprise architecture; 05 determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 implementing, maintaining and scaling. Beside them a grid of tiles names resources for each phase, marked as PDF for print or online environment; among them the WHO-ITU national eHealth strategy toolkit, the Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG), WHO guideline recommendations on digital interventions, Open Health Information Exchange, TOGAF, and a highlighted tile 'WHO SMART guidelines: digital adaptation kits (this document) and machine-readable recommendations' in phase 05. Source: adapted from WHO (reference 1).

vfig-p040.saw: Fig. 4, a two-lane process overview of workflows A-I
vfig-p040.draft: Fig. 4, 'Overview of key immunization processes'. Two swimlanes. Vaccination location management holds A. vaccination location registration, G. resolve duplicate client records, H. resolve duplicate vaccination events, I. report generation, and a grey 'Supply chain management' box not covered by this kit. Vaccination location runs from Start through B. plan service delivery into a Service Delivery area: C. client registration, D. administer vaccine, then 'All vaccine series complete?'; yes ends the process, no leads to E. client reminder and 'Overdue for a dose?', where yes leads to F. defaulter tracing and no to the end. Each workflow box carries a subprocess marker.

vfig-p058.draft: Fig. 9, 'Workflow E: client reminder business process'. Two lanes: electronic immunization registry, and vaccination location health worker. From Start the health worker does 1. define/evaluate criteria and 2. select notification method; the registry does 3. generate list of clients and 4. send notifications. vfig-p064.saw: Fig. 11, a two-lane process for resolving duplicate client records
vfig-p064.draft: Fig. 11, 'Workflow G: resolve duplicate client records business process'. Two lanes: PCPOSS, and vaccination location health worker or system administrator. The PCPOSS does 1. flag client records for evaluation and 2. produce list of potential duplicate records; the person does 3. perform manual review and decides 4. can records be merged? Yes leads to 5. merge records in the PCPOSS; no leads to 6. mark as 'not a duplicate' or 'pending'. Both end the process.

vfig-p066.saw: Fig. 12, a two-lane process for resolving duplicate vaccination events
vfig-p066.draft: Fig. 12, 'Workflow H: resolve duplicate vaccination events business process'. Two lanes: PCPOSS, and vaccination location health worker or system administrator. The PCPOSS does 1. identify groups of vaccination events for evaluation; the person does 2. evaluate vaccination event records and decides 3. duplicate events? No ends the process; yes leads to 4. select the most accurate/suitable event record, then the PCPOSS does 5. update vaccination event records and 6. generate report of duplicate vaccination events, and the process ends.

vfig-p068.saw: Fig. 13, a two-lane process for generating reports
vfig-p068.draft: Fig. 13, 'Workflow I: report generation business process'. Two lanes: vaccination location health worker, and PCPOSS. From Start the health worker does 1. define parameters for report; the PCPOSS does 2. generate report; the health worker does 3. high level review and decides 4. report acceptable? No loops back to step 1; yes leads to 5. analyse, and the process ends.

vfig-p036.saw: Figure 3, a four-lane Continuity of Care workflow with every path shown
vfig-p036.draft: Figure 3, 'Continuity of Care scenario': the vaccine is administered, the core data set is recorded on the DDCC paper certificate, and the record is then made available in digital form. Four lanes: subject of care, vaccinator, data entry personnel, DDCC holder. (1) The subject of care arrives at the care site; (2) the vaccinator vaccinates and (3) records core data set elements on a paper certificate, which the holder receives as Point A, a paper record of DDCC:VS. Is there a digital health solution at the care site? If no, (5) data entry personnel record the elements in a digital health solution. If yes, (4) the vaccinator records them in one; then, does the care site have Internet connectivity? Yes leads directly, and no via step 5, to Point B: the record of vaccination status is available in a digital form. End.

vfig-p038.saw: Figure 4, the Figure 3 workflow with the Paper First path highlighted and the rest greyed
vfig-p038.draft: Figure 4, 'Continuity of Care scenario: Paper First use case (UC001)'. The Figure 3 workflow with one path highlighted: arrival (1), vaccination (2), recording on the paper certificate (3) which gives Point A, then no digital health solution at the care site, so data entry personnel record the data in a digital health solution (5), reaching Point B, the record available in digital form. Step 4 and the connectivity decision are greyed out.

vfig-p039.saw: Figure 5, the Figure 3 workflow with the Offline Digital path highlighted
vfig-p039.draft: Figure 5, 'Continuity of Care scenario: Offline Digital use case (UC002)'. The Figure 3 workflow with one path highlighted: arrival (1), vaccination (2), paper recording (3) giving Point A; a digital health solution is at the care site, so the vaccinator records the data in it (4); the site has no Internet connectivity, so data entry personnel record the data (5), reaching Point B. The direct 'no digital solution' and 'connected' branches are greyed out.

vfig-p040.saw: Figure 6, the Figure 3 workflow with the Online Digital path highlighted
vfig-p040.draft: Figure 6, 'Continuity of Care scenario: Online Digital use case (UC003)'. The Figure 3 workflow with one path highlighted: arrival (1), vaccination (2), paper recording (3) giving Point A; a digital health solution is at the care site and the vaccinator records the data in it (4); the site has Internet connectivity, so the record goes directly to Point B, available in digital form. Step 5 by data entry personnel is greyed out.

vfig-p046.saw: Figure 7, five services joined by labelled arrows, some dashed and optional
vfig-p046.draft: Figure 7, 'The relationships between digital services for Proof of Vaccination'. A digital health solution submits a vaccination event to the DDCC:VS generation service, which returns a DDCC:VS. The HCID is provided by an existing national system or issued by the generation service. The generation service registers the DDCC:VS with the DDCC:VS registry service and may optionally store it in a DDCC:VS repository. Optional dashed links: an online status check between the registry service and the repository, and online verification of a DDCC:VS between an optional status checking application and the registry service. A note explains that the HCID, the unique identifier in a DDCC:VS, is used throughout these services and lets verifiers search for and retrieve a DDCC:VS.

vfig-p048.saw: Figure 8, a four-lane Proof of Vaccination workflow with every path shown
vfig-p048.draft: Figure 8, 'Proof of Vaccination scenario': verification of a claim of vaccination. Four lanes: DDCC holder, verifier, national PHA, international PHA. (1) The holder presents the DDCC:VS; (2) the verifier receives the claim. Is cryptographic verification required? No leads straight to Point C, the decision on the verification. Yes: (3) the verifier uses a status checking application; perform check online? No leads to Point C. Yes: (4) the national PHA performs an online check with its DDCC registry service; check with international PHA? If yes, (5) the international PHA performs an online check with its registry service; either way (6) results are communicated back to the verifier, then Point C and End.

vfig-p050.saw: Figure 9, the Figure 8 workflow with only the manual-verification path highlighted
vfig-p050.draft: Figure 9, 'Proof of Vaccination scenario: Manual Verification use case (UC004)'. The Figure 8 workflow with one path highlighted: the holder presents the DDCC:VS (1), the verifier receives the claim (2), no cryptographic verification is required, and the verifier goes directly to Point C, the decision on the claim. All the status-checking and PHA steps are greyed out.

vfig-p051.saw: Figure 10, the Figure 8 workflow with the offline cryptographic path highlighted
vfig-p051.draft: Figure 10, 'Proof of Vaccination scenario: Offline Cryptographic Verification use case (UC005)'. The Figure 8 workflow with one path highlighted: presentation (1), receipt of the claim (2), cryptographic verification required, the verifier uses a status checking application (3) and does not check online, going to Point C. The online PHA checks are greyed out.

vfig-p052.saw: Figure 11, the Figure 8 workflow with the national online status check highlighted
vfig-p052.draft: Figure 11, 'Proof of Vaccination scenario: Online Status Check (National DDCC:VS) use case (UC006)'. The Figure 8 workflow with one path highlighted: presentation (1), receipt (2), cryptographic verification required, status checking application (3), online check performed by the national PHA against its DDCC registry service (4), no international check, results communicated back to the verifier (6), Point C. vfig-p053.saw: Figure 12, the Figure 8 workflow with the international online status check highlighted

vfig-p064.saw: Figure 13, three certificate boxes with a numbered signing arc above and a dotted verifying arc below
vfig-p064.draft: Figure 13, 'The chain of trust'. Three linked boxes: CSCA (country signing certificate authority) and DSC (document signer certificate), each with a private and a public key, and DDCC (Digital Documentation of COVID-19 Certificate), marked with a QR code. Above, 'Signing and issuing a DDCC' runs in steps 1-3 from CSCA through DSC to DDCC. Below, a dotted 'Verifying a DDCC' arc runs in steps 1-3 the other way, from DDCC back to CSCA.

vfig-p065.draft: Figure 14, 'How digital signatures work', under the heading Document Signing. A signer starts from a document (vaccination data); a hash is calculated from the document, giving the document hash; the hash is digitally signed with a private key, giving the signed hash; the signed hash is added to the document, giving a document with a digitally signed hash (the DDCC:VS).

vfig-p066.saw: Figure 15, the signing flow above a validation flow
vfig-p066.draft: Figure 15, 'How digital signature verification works'. The upper panel, Document Signing, repeats Figure 14: document, document hash, signed with the private key, signed hash added to the document to make the DDCC:VS. The signer sends the digitally signed document and the public key to the verifier. The lower panel, Document Validation: the verifier calculates a hash from the document and, using the public key, obtains the hash from the signed hash; the two values are compared, and a matching hash indicates a valid document, one that contains the information that was signed with the private key.

vfig-p022.saw: Figure 3, the health labour market framework diagram showing the flow from the education sector through labour market dynamics to universal health coverage, with four policy intervention boxes below
vfig-p022.draft: Figure 3, "The health labour market framework". Across the top runs a banner for "Economy, population and broader societal drivers". Below it, the diagram divides into "Education sector" on the left and "Labour market dynamics" on the right. In the education sector, "High school" branches into "Education in health" and "Education in other fields". "Education in health" feeds the "Pool of qualified health workers" (with two-way "Migration" to and from "Abroad"), which in turn splits into "Employed", "Unemployed" and "Out of labour force". "Employed" flows into the "Health care sector" and "Other sectors" (which also receives workers from education in other fields). The "Health care sector" produces a "Health workforce equipped to deliver quality health service", leading to "Universal health coverage with safe, effective, person-centred health services". Beneath the flow sit three policy boxes aligned with the stages — "Policies on production" (on infrastructure and material, enrolment, selecting students, teaching staff), "Policies to address inflows and outflows" (to address migration and emigration, attract unemployed health workers, bring health workers back into the health care sector), and "Policies to address maldistribution and inefficiencies" (to improve productivity and performance, improve skill mix composition, retain health workers in underserved areas) — all spanned at the bottom by a fourth box, "Policies to regulate the private sector" (to manage dual practice, improve quality of training, enhance service delivery).

vfig-p016.draft: Figure 1, ‘The health labour market framework’. At the top, a wide bar ‘Economy, population and broader societal drivers’ sends downward arrows into two main domains: ‘Education sector’ (left, orange) and ‘Labour market dynamics’ (right, pink/blue). Beneath the flow, three policy boxes point upward to their respective stages — ‘Policies on production’ (infrastructure and material, enrolment, selecting students, teaching staff), ‘Policies to address inflows and outflows’ (migration and emigration, attracting unemployed health workers, bringing health workers back into the health care sector), and ‘Policies to address maldistribution and inefficiencies’ (productivity and performance, skill mix composition, retaining health workers in underserved areas) — above a full-width bottom bar, ‘Policies to regulate the private sector’ (manage dual practice, improve quality of training, enhance service delivery).

vfig-p028.saw: Fig. 10, a stacked vertical bar chart of the cumulative volume of data points across nine key HWF topics by data release year from 2018 to 2025
vfig-p028.draft: Fig. 10, ‘Trend of data volume for key HWF topics in the NHWA data platform by year of data release’. A stacked vertical bar chart showing total data points (vertical axis 0 to 300 000) across annual releases from 2018 to 2025, broken down by nine topics: Stock, Activity level, Sex, Age group, Place of birth, Place of training, Facility ownership, Facility type, and Graduates. Total volume grows nearly 20-fold from 12 587 data points in 2018 (stock data only) to 248 873 data points in 2025 across all nine topics.

vfig-p040.saw: Fig. 16, a stacked horizontal age-pyramid bar chart showing 2024 population size in thousands by five-year age group and World Bank income group
vfig-p040.draft: Fig. 16, ‘Age population pyramid by World Bank income group in 2024, expressed as population size in 1000s by income group’ (Source: UN World Population Prospects 2024). A horizontal stacked bar chart plotting five-year age cohorts from 0–4 up to 100+ against population size in thousands (0 to 350 000 on each side), disaggregated into Low-income, Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, and High-income countries (World Bank FY 2026 classification).

vfig-p042.saw: Fig. 17, a two-panel grouped horizontal bar chart showing the age distribution of (a) medical doctors and (b) nursing personnel across six age brackets by World Bank income group
vfig-p042.draft: Fig. 17, ‘Age distribution of (a) medical doctors and (b) nursing personnel, by income group’ (Source: WHO National Health Workforce Accounts, 2025, latest available data for 122 countries for medical doctors and 142 countries for nursing personnel over 2015–2024). Two grouped horizontal bar charts showing the percentage of the workforce in six age brackets (<25, 25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64, and 65+) across Low-income, Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, and High-income countries for (a) medical doctors (0.0% to 50.0% scale) and (b) nursing personnel (0.0% to 50.0% scale).

vfig-p044.saw: Fig. 18, a two-panel scatter plot comparing the percentage aged under 35 against the percentage aged 55 and over for (a) medical doctors and (b) nursing personnel by country income group
vfig-p044.draft: Fig. 18, ‘Relative proportions of (a) medical doctors and (b) nursing personnel aged over 55 years and below 35 years, by income group’ (Source: WHO National Health Workforce Accounts, 2025, latest available data over 2015–2024). Two scatter plots — panel (a) for medical doctors and panel (b) for nursing personnel — plotting each country’s percentage aged <35 on the horizontal axis (0% to 80%) against its percentage aged 55+ on the vertical axis (0% to 60%), colour-coded by World Bank FY 2026 income group (Low-income, Lower-middle-income, Upper-middle-income, and High-income countries), with a diagonal equality line indicating where the share of workers near retirement (55+) equals the share of young workers (<35).

img-p026-1.saw: a black-and-white photo on the Core competency 1 divider page
img-p026-1.draft: Black-and-white photograph of a health worker wearing a face mask and gloves, holding up a small labelled sample tube towards the camera. It illustrates the divider page for Core competency 1 on the boundary between public health practice (including surveillance) and research.

translations.ar: صورة فوتوغرافية بالأبيض والأسود لعاملة صحية ترتدي كمامة وقفازين وترفع أنبوب عينة صغيراً عليه ملصق نحو الكاميرا. وتوضّح الصورة صفحة الفصل الخاصة بالكفاءة الأساسية 1 بشأن الحدود بين ممارسة الصحة العمومية (بما في ذلك الترصد) والبحث.
translations.zh: 黑白照片：一名戴口罩和手套的卫生工作人员向镜头举起一支贴有标签的小样本管。该照片用于核心能力1（区分公共卫生实践（包括监测）与研究之间界限）的章节扉页。
translations.es: Fotografía en blanco y negro de una trabajadora de salud con mascarilla y guantes que sostiene hacia la cámara un pequeño tubo de muestra etiquetado. Ilustra la página divisoria de la competencia básica 1, sobre el límite entre la práctica de salud pública (incluida la vigilancia) y la investigación.
translations.fr: Photographie en noir et blanc d’une agente de santé portant un masque et des gants, qui tient vers l’objectif un petit tube d’échantillon étiqueté. Elle illustre la page de séparation de la compétence essentielle 1, relative à la limite entre la pratique de santé publique (y compris la surveillance) et la recherche.
translations.ru: Черно-белая фотография медицинской работницы в маске и перчатках, которая держит перед камерой небольшую пробирку с этикеткой. Фотография иллюстрирует титульную страницу раздела «Основная компетенция 1» о границе между практикой общественного здравоохранения (включая эпиднадзор) и исследованиями.

img-p064-1.draft: Black-and-white photograph of a group of people seated around U-shaped tables in a meeting room, some reading and writing on papers. It illustrates the divider page for Core competency 2 on determining appropriate ethical review procedures for interventions, surveillance and research during emergencies.

translations.ar: صورة فوتوغرافية بالأبيض والأسود لمجموعة من الأشخاص يجلسون حول طاولات على شكل حرف U في قاعة اجتماعات، ويقرأ بعضهم أوراقاً ويكتب عليها. وتوضّح الصورة صفحة الفصل الخاصة بالكفاءة الأساسية 2 بشأن تحديد إجراءات الاستعراض الأخلاقي المناسبة للتدخلات والترصد والبحث أثناء الطوارئ.
translations.zh: 黑白照片：一群人围坐在会议室的U形会议桌旁，有些人在阅读文件或做记录。该照片用于核心能力2（在突发事件期间实施公共卫生干预、监测和研究时确定适当的伦理审查程序）的章节扉页。
translations.es: Fotografía en blanco y negro de un grupo de personas sentadas alrededor de mesas dispuestas en U en una sala de reuniones; algunas leen y escriben en papeles. Ilustra la página divisoria de la competencia básica 2, sobre la determinación de los procedimientos de examen ético adecuados para intervenciones, vigilancia e investigación durante emergencias.
translations.fr: Photographie en noir et blanc d’un groupe de personnes assises autour de tables disposées en U dans une salle de réunion, certaines lisant ou écrivant sur des documents. Elle illustre la page de séparation de la compétence essentielle 2, relative à la détermination des procédures d’examen éthique appropriées pour les interventions, la surveillance et la recherche en situation d’urgence.
translations.ru: Черно-белая фотография группы людей, сидящих за П-образно расставленными столами в зале заседаний; некоторые читают и делают записи. Фотография иллюстрирует титульную страницу раздела «Основная компетенция 2» об определении надлежащих процедур этической экспертизы для вмешательств, эпиднадзора и исследований в чрезвычайных ситуациях.

img-p092-1.saw: a captioned photo of Ebola house disinfection, DRC 2007
img-p092-1.draft: Black-and-white photograph of a worker in full protective clothing spraying disinfectant in the foreground while women and children stand watching in front of a reed fence. The embedded caption says local health workers, working with experts from Médecins Sans Frontières, are disinfecting the house of a person who died of Ebola virus disease, Democratic Republic of the Congo, 2007 (source: WHO/Christopher Black).

translations.ar: صورة فوتوغرافية بالأبيض والأسود لعامل يرتدي ملابس واقية كاملة ويرش مطهّراً في مقدمة الصورة، بينما تقف نساء وأطفال يراقبون أمام سياج من القصب. ويذكر التعليق المضمّن أن عاملين صحيين محليين، بالتعاون مع خبراء من منظمة أطباء بلا حدود، يطهّرون منزل شخص توفي بسبب مرض فيروس الإيبولا، جمهورية الكونغو الديمقراطية، 2007 (المصدر: WHO/Christopher Black).
translations.zh: 黑白照片：前景中一名身穿全套防护服的工作人员正在喷洒消毒剂，妇女和儿童站在芦苇篱笆前观看。图中说明文字为：当地卫生工作人员与来自“无国界医生”的专家一起工作，对死于埃博拉病毒病患者的房子进行消毒。刚果民主共和国，2007年（来源：WHO/Christopher Black）。
translations.es: Fotografía en blanco y negro de un trabajador con equipo de protección completo que rocía desinfectante en primer plano, mientras mujeres y niños observan de pie delante de una cerca de cañas. El pie de foto integrado indica que trabajadores de salud locales, junto con expertos de Médicos Sin Fronteras, desinfectan la casa de una persona fallecida por la enfermedad por el virus del Ebola, República Democrática del Congo, 2007 (fuente: WHO/Christopher Black).
translations.fr: Photographie en noir et blanc d’un intervenant en tenue de protection intégrale pulvérisant du désinfectant au premier plan, tandis que des femmes et des enfants regardent, debout devant une clôture de roseaux. La légende intégrée indique que des agents de santé locaux, avec des experts de Médecins Sans Frontières, désinfectent la maison d’une personne décédée de la maladie à virus Ebola, République démocratique du Congo, 2007 (source : WHO/Christopher Black).
translations.ru: Черно-белая фотография: на переднем плане работник в полном защитном костюме распыляет дезинфицирующее средство, а женщины и дети стоят и наблюдают перед тростниковой оградой. Встроенная подпись гласит, что местные медицинские работники вместе с экспертами организации «Врачи без границ» дезинфицируют дом человека, умершего от болезни, вызванной вирусом Эбола, Демократическая Республика Конго, 2007 г. (источник: WHO/Christopher Black).

img-p168-1.saw: a collage of ethics and public health journal covers
img-p168-1.draft: Black-and-white collage of overlapping journal covers: the Weekly epidemiological record / Relevé épidémiologique hebdomadaire, Public Health Ethics (Volume 1, Number 1, January 2008), the Bulletin of the World Health Organization, Monash Bioethics Review and Asian Bioethics Review. It illustrates the divider page for Core competency 5 on the relationship between public health surveillance or emergency research and publication ethics.

translations.ar: مجموعة صور بالأبيض والأسود لأغلفة مجلات متداخلة: السجل الوبائي الأسبوعي (Weekly epidemiological record / Relevé épidémiologique hebdomadaire)، ومجلة Public Health Ethics (المجلد 1، العدد 1، كانون الثاني/يناير 2008)، ونشرة منظمة الصحة العالمية، ومجلة Monash Bioethics Review، ومجلة Asian Bioethics Review. وتوضّح الصورة صفحة الفصل الخاصة بالكفاءة الأساسية 5 بشأن العلاقة بين ترصد الصحة العمومية أو البحث في حالات الطوارئ وأخلاقيات النشر.
translations.zh: 黑白拼贴图，展示若干相互重叠的期刊封面：《疫情周报》（Weekly epidemiological record / Relevé épidémiologique hebdomadaire）、《Public Health Ethics》（第1卷第1期，2008年1月）、《世界卫生组织简报》、《Monash Bioethics Review》和《Asian Bioethics Review》。该图用于核心能力5（解释公共卫生监测或紧急情况下研究与出版伦理之间关系）的章节扉页。
translations.es: Collage en blanco y negro de portadas de revistas superpuestas: el Weekly epidemiological record / Relevé épidémiologique hebdomadaire, Public Health Ethics (volumen 1, número 1, enero de 2008), el Boletín de la Organización Mundial de la Salud, Monash Bioethics Review y Asian Bioethics Review. Ilustra la página divisoria de la competencia básica 5, sobre la relación entre la vigilancia de salud pública o la investigación en emergencias y la ética de la publicación.
translations.fr: Collage en noir et blanc de couvertures de revues superposées : le Weekly epidemiological record / Relevé épidémiologique hebdomadaire, Public Health Ethics (volume 1, numéro 1, janvier 2008), le Bulletin de l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé, Monash Bioethics Review et Asian Bioethics Review. Il illustre la page de séparation de la compétence essentielle 5, relative au lien entre la surveillance de santé publique ou la recherche en situation d’urgence et l’éthique de la publication.
translations.ru: Черно-белый коллаж из перекрывающихся обложек журналов: Weekly epidemiological record / Relevé épidémiologique hebdomadaire, Public Health Ethics (том 1, номер 1, январь 2008 г.), Бюллетень Всемирной организации здравоохранения, Monash Bioethics Review и Asian Bioethics Review. Коллаж иллюстрирует титульную страницу раздела «Основная компетенция 5» о взаимосвязи между эпиднадзором в области общественного здравоохранения или исследованиями в чрезвычайных ситуациях и этикой публикаций.

img-p172-1.saw: Figure 1, a diagram of research to improve health systems (Remme et al., 2010)
img-p172-1.draft: Diagram in three horizontal bands showing research to improve health systems (Figure 1, after Remme et al., 2010). The top band, research domains, shows nested brackets of increasing size for operational, implementation and health systems research; the middle band, research users, places health care workers, programme managers and health system managers/policy-makers under them; the bottom band, research application, is a wedge widening from local to broad.

translations.ar: مخطط من ثلاثة أشرطة أفقية يبيّن البحوث الرامية إلى تحسين النظم الصحية (الشكل 1، نقلاً عن Remme وآخرين، 2010). ويعرض الشريط العلوي، مجالات البحث، أقواساً متداخلة متزايدة الحجم للبحوث التشغيلية وبحوث التنفيذ وبحوث النظم الصحية؛ ويضع الشريط الأوسط، مستخدمو البحوث، تحتها العاملين في مجال الرعاية الصحية ومديري البرامج ومديري النظم الصحية/صانعي السياسات؛ أما الشريط السفلي، تطبيق البحوث، فهو إسفين يتسع من النطاق المحلي إلى النطاق الواسع.
translations.zh: 由三个横向条带组成的示意图，展示改善卫生系统的研究（图1，引自Remme et al.，2010）。上方条带“研究领域”以逐渐增大的嵌套括号表示操作、实施和卫生系统研究；中间条带“研究用户”对应列出卫生保健人员、项目主管和卫生系统主管/决策者；下方条带“研究应用”为一个从“局部”逐渐扩展到“广阔”的楔形。
translations.es: Diagrama en tres franjas horizontales que muestra la investigación para mejorar los sistemas de salud (figura 1, según Remme et al., 2010). La franja superior, ámbitos de investigación, muestra corchetes anidados de tamaño creciente para la investigación operativa, la investigación sobre la ejecución y la investigación sobre sistemas de salud; la franja central, usuarios de la investigación, sitúa debajo a los trabajadores de salud, los gestores de programas y los gestores de sistemas de salud/responsables de políticas; la franja inferior, aplicación de la investigación, es una cuña que se ensancha de local a amplia.
translations.fr: Schéma en trois bandes horizontales présentant la recherche visant à améliorer les systèmes de santé (figure 1, d’après Remme et al., 2010). La bande supérieure, domaines de recherche, montre des crochets imbriqués de taille croissante pour la recherche opérationnelle, la recherche sur la mise en œuvre et la recherche sur les systèmes de santé ; la bande centrale, utilisateurs de la recherche, place en regard les agents de santé, les gestionnaires de programmes et les gestionnaires des systèmes de santé/décideurs ; la bande inférieure, application de la recherche, est un coin qui s’élargit du local au général.
translations.ru: Схема из трех горизонтальных полос, отражающая исследования для улучшения систем здравоохранения (рисунок 1, по Remme et al., 2010). Верхняя полоса, «области исследований», показывает вложенные скобки возрастающего размера для операционных исследований, исследований по внедрению и исследований систем здравоохранения; средняя полоса, «пользователи исследований», соотносит с ними медицинских работников, руководителей программ и руководителей систем здравоохранения/лиц, определяющих политику; нижняя полоса, «применение исследований», представляет собой клин, расширяющийся от местного к широкому.

translations.es: Fotografía nocturna en blanco y negro de una trabajadora de salud arrodillada junto a un paciente tendido en el suelo, entre muchos otros pacientes, en una zona de tratamiento al aire libre.
